articles.title_orig: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.title_zh: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.content_orig:
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace , and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5 , each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge , which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.
Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.
He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.
“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.
“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”
Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.
“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”
He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.
On the same day, Denmark took action on a separate front. It announced that it was expelling Russia’s defence attache after Danish intelligence concluded that Moscow had orchestrated a plot to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner during a concert near Copenhagen.

articles.title_orig: US House Select Committee on China Report Says Western Aerospace Firms Transferred Technology to Chinese Firms
articles.title_zh: US House Select Committee on China Report Says Western Aerospace Firms Transferred Technology to Chinese Firms
articles.content_orig:
Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.
China's military could exploit advanced American technology, including through espionage and unauthorized access to artificial intelligence infrastructure, to develop weapons that could ultimately threaten U.S. forces, two congressional China watchdog leaders warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.
The officials raised concerns that Beijing is seeking to acquire sophisticated U.S. semiconductors and access powerful AI data centers, potentially strengthening its military capabilities without the knowledge or involvement of the American companies behind the technology.
Those concerns are underscored by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's 2026 annual report , which says Beijing is seeking to circumvent American export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors for military modernization.
BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN
Racks of GPUs with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center in Indonesia on Feb. 4, 2026. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images)
Citing an April 2026 assessment by Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, the commission reported that China's People's Liberation Army was soliciting advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled military capabilities.
The report describes Beijing's push toward "intelligentized warfare," integrating AI into weapons systems, targeting, military command and logistics.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, warned that the threat extends beyond chip exports to access to computing infrastructure abroad. "Anytime the Chinese gain access to advanced chips, we are helping them," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
Commission Chairman Randall Schriver acknowledged the risk, pointing to permitted sales of dual-use technology, inadequate cybersecurity protections and American investments.
"I think we need sort of a comprehensive look at how the Americans are either wittingly or unwittingly contributing to Chinese military modernization," Schriver said.
Kuiken warned that Chinese AI developers or military institutions could also gain access to powerful data centers. "If we're doing it knowingly, we need to bring it to an end," he said.
TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China, making the company’s technology a focal point in the U.S.-China race for AI leadership. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The warnings come amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's relationship with China . Reuters reported Nov. 18, 2026, that Nvidia had stopped shipping licensed Hopper-generation AI data center chips to Chinese customers, according to interim CEO Colette Kress.
The findings also come amid a separate controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned in November following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , whom U.S. authorities have suspected of having intelligence ties to Beijing.
Jensen Huang has denied knowing about her alleged intelligence connections, while Beijing has rejected the espionage accusations. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation. U.S. authorities have not conclusively established that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing, and Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegations.
The commissioners also warned that China's advances extend beyond acquiring American hardware.
"Denial and deception is part of the CCP's standing doctrine, and that extends to the PLA, so I'm sure there are things we have yet to discover," Schriver said.
FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL
He pointed to China's growing use of AI-enabled military systems, including autonomous unmanned platforms.
Kuiken warned that Beijing is increasingly integrating advanced AI into existing military technology. "We are absolutely seeing the PLA take the technologies that they have on the shelf today and figuring out how they can deploy the most advanced artificial intelligence capabilities into that ecosystem so that they can gain advantage," he said.
Against those concerns, China's Foreign Ministry struck a more cooperative tone regarding AI security in a Nov. 19, 2026, statement following a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
China's first AI-powered soccer tournament (CCTV)
CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT
"China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination, prevent the security risks of AI, and ensure that AI is always under human control," the ministry said in its account of Xi's remarks.
The commission also identifies protecting American data as a leading national security priority, warning that AI could make it easier to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and compromise sensitive information, amid a series of high-profile technology outages affecting major U.S. companies and government systems.
Asked about the recent disruptions involving the NSA, Apple and Chase Bank, Kuiken warned that increasingly sophisticated AI models are making it easier to identify cybersecurity weaknesses .
"These frontier models are incredibly good at cyber, which means they're good at coding and coding means it's very easy to find vulnerabilities in things," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. "You're basically seeing these leading organizations around the world do everything they can to lock down their organizations to make sure they're not vulnerable."
Kuiken emphasized that the commission's leading recommendation this year focuses on protecting American data, describing it as both a national security priority and an economic resource. "One, we want to protect it to keep ourselves secure and two, we wanna deploy it in the models that we have with the democratic world, controls to get economic benefit from it," he said.
The commissioners did not establish any connection between the recent technology outages and Chinese cyber operations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
An Amazon Web Services data center on Aug. 26, 2026, in Stone Ridge, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended Beijing's technological development and criticized U.S. export restrictions. "China’s sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," the spokesperson said. "China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues, opposes abuse of export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serve no one’s interests."
"China and the U.S. need to work together to deliver on the important common understandings between the two presidents and uphold the momentum of steady development of China-U.S. economic and trade ties," the spokesperson added.
The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

articles.title_orig: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
articles.title_zh: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month.
Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January , as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates .
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates.
Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges , the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
articles.content_orig:
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro is in intensive care after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction, according to the DF Star hospital where he is being treated.
Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted on Friday with abdominal pain. In a bulletin on Saturday, the hospital said doctors have started giving him fluids and nutritional support, and inserted a tube into his stomach.
It said the former president is clinically stable and conscious, although they said there was no projected date for his discharge.
“There is hope that his condition will improve,” his son, Senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, wrote on X on Saturday afternoon. “He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus.”
In the early hours of Saturday morning, he described his father’s difficult night of treatment, where food residue was removed from his stomach using a tube inserted into his nose, and bouts of nausea.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote, suggesting that his father might need another surgery, which would be his 10th in less than eight years.
“All this is happening to a man sentenced to 27 years in prison without having committed any crime, while criminals do whatever they want with what’s left of this country,” the younger Bolsonaro continued.
Bolsonaro has been serving a 27-year sentence since last year for an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro has denied the charges.
He has been hospitalised repeatedly and has had to undergo surgeries after being stabbed in 2018 during a campaign event.
He was transferred in March to house arrest after spending several months in jail because of his health issues.
Next month, Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to consider the constitutionality of a law that changes how sentences are calculated, which could shorten his sentence and those of others convicted in the 2022 coup plot.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship ablaze in Baltic Sea after drone strike, crew evacuates
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship ablaze in Baltic Sea after drone strike, crew evacuates
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

Vladimir Putinâs crusade to win over war veterans has been brutally exposed as a farce by members of his own party.
The Russian leaderâs âTime of Heroesâ program has, since its inception in early 2024, sought to put a romanticized spin on the Kremlinâs war against Ukraine and the meat grinder tactics used by the military to keep feeding the war machine, signaling to both military veterans and the wider Russian public that those who have served on the battlefield will serve as the countryâs new âeliteâ and hold prestigious places in government.
That notion went up in flames this week after two local lawmakers from Putinâs United Russia party were caught using their supposed enthusiasm for the program to lure vulnerable men into a deranged scheme. After forcing the men to sign contracts to join the war, they arranged quick marriages before deployment and set up bank accounts to receive âdeath benefitsâ for their newlywed husbandsâ inevitable battlefield demise.
Irina Bezman showed off her new husband in a social media post nodding to the "time of heroes."
Federal investigators in Krasnoyarsk Krai detailed the bizarre plot in a press release announcing the chargesâthough they neglected to mention that two of the suspects were the face of Putinâs local âTime of Heroesâ program as deputies of United Russia.
The group first stole a one-time payment issued to one of the men for his military service in the amount of 1.8 million rubles ($22,000), and âfollowing the death of the service member, the group stole another 5 million rubles from his bank account,â investigators said.
They reportedly failed to get access to the bank account of the other duped groom.
The two women, identified in local reports as 41-year-old Irina Bezman and 64-year-old Galina Kalimulina, worked as deputies of the Sharypovo District Council and routinely posted about their support for the war.
It was one of their social media posts that reportedly triggered local scrutiny: Bezman, in a now-deleted post, shared a photo of herself with her new husband, Vladimir, holding up their marriage certificate at the local registration office.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (C), Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev (L) and Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu (R) attend a wreath laying ceremony at the tomb of the unknown soldier to mark the Defender of the Fatheland Day on February 23, 2015 in central Moscow, Russia.

The local outlet Zapad24 reports that residents were immediately baffled to see the local councilwoman had married a man from a very different walk of life, known mainly for hanging out on a local churchâs steps and sweeping the courtyard.
Kalimulina, who had served as the executive secretary of the regional branch of United Russia, was described as the mastermind of the scheme.
She filled her social media pages with posts in support of the war and Russian troops, often signing off on them with the hashtag âWe donât abandon our own.â

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.content_orig:
Bahrain's interior ministry said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a civilian industrial facility, sparking a fire and causing material damage, though no injuries were reported.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site. Civil Defence is working to bring the fire under control," the interior ministry said on X .
"Preliminary reports indicate material damage, with no injuries reported," it added, without specifying the site's location.
Bahrain is host of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
A U.S. official told CBS News that Iran launched new attack attempts, but there were no impacts to U.S. forces or military assets in the region.
This latest incident marks the fourth attempted attack by Iran in Bahrain in roughly a week, a sharp escalation following a relative lull of about two months in attacks linked to Iran on U.S.-associated targets in the Gulf.
Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details.
Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television.
"At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves."
Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.
Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.
The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days.
President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future.
"What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon."
Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since.
Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with.
"I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said.
Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles.
The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles' speed and trajectory.
The location of the missile site was not revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran's missile capabilities and counter past U.S. claims to have destroyed the missile program, amid fears that the war with the United States could heat up once again.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard's Aerospace Force, boasted that Iran's "capabilities have expanded significantly," adding, "We have integrated 'surprises' and highly effective assets into our combat structure."
Two tankers were attacked on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States, British maritime agency UKMTO said.
"A tanker transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz has been hit on the stern by an unknown projectile. There are no reported casualties at this time," the agency said, adding that another tanker was struck in its engine room.
Also on Saturday, Iran said it shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the strait, according to Iranian state TV.
American fighter jets struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm last Tuesday, according to a U.S. military official.
Before the Middle East war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, one fifth of the world's oil and natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has since locked down the strait and regularly targets ships that attempt to pass without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and its navy has been escorting tankers through the waterway.
Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.title_zh: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.content_orig:
High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!
Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!
This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).
At this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.
The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.
Looking at the best sellers in several size categories , the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.
Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.
Considering that 56% of the new SUVs launched this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).
Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.
Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:
A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000) . This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the new generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.
BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the new generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations . Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?
BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations , which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles currently having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.
Things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations , the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….
After the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.
Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?
As for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!
Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.
Still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6 , the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!
A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also new VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?
Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s new baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi S

articles.content_orig:
TEHRAN — An image published this week by the website of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei showed a missile-shaped clock hand pointing toward the 4,500–5,000-kilometer range markers, accompanied by the new leader's recent instruction that any response to an attack should be "immediate, effective and without geographical boundaries."
Coming days after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that Iran had lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer (1,243-mile) missile-range restriction, the graphic signaled a significant change in the leadership's public posture. Senior military officials have since portrayed the war not as a setback for Iran's military ambitions but as an opportunity to accelerate them.
On Friday, IRGC commander Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi told a group of students in Tehran that the force's Aerospace Division was producing new achievements "one after another," adding that its strength was "undoubtedly greater than in the first war." According to Tasnim news agency, Vahidi claimed that the IRGC enjoyed "initiatives and operational capabilities" and was currently working on "epic" products.
The statements point to a strategic calculation taking shape under Mojtaba Khamenei: the war exposed the vulnerability of Iran's military infrastructure, but also reinforced the leadership's conviction that it needs a more powerful and geographically expansive deterrent.

articles.title_orig: A 36,000-foot-rated underwater robot modeled on a deep-sea fish can land on the seafloor, take samples and map it in 3D, is light enough for a small team to launch from an ordinary research ship, and already went about 19,700 feet down off Bermuda ahead
articles.title_zh: A 36,000-foot-rated underwater robot modeled on a deep-sea fish can land on the seafloor, take samples and map it in 3D, is light enough for a small team to launch from an ordinary research ship, and already went about 19,700 feet down off Bermuda ahead
articles.content_orig:
A seat aboard Alvin is one of the harder tickets to get in ocean science. The three-person submarine fits a pilot and two scientists, and over its career it’s carried more than 3,000 researchers on more than 5,000 dives. That sounds like plenty until you remember it’s only ever two scientists at a time.
So you’d want a pretty good idea of what’s down there before you spend one of those dives. That’s basically the job the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution gave its newest underwater robot back in June, months before it officially showed the thing off.
WHOI unveiled Deep Venture on November 20. It’s an autonomous underwater vehicle, or AUV, built with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, and it’s rated for about 36,000 feet. WHOI calls that full ocean depth. In plain English, it’s designed to work anywhere on the seafloor, trenches included.
It’s also surprisingly small. According to the WHOI announcement , it weighs about 550 pounds and it’s roughly 6 feet long. WHOI’s own pages don’t quite agree on the rest (the release says 60 inches wide and 56 tall, while the vehicle page lists 39 by 51), so I’d treat the width and height as a ballpark.
In June, WHOI took Deep Venture out near Bermuda alongside Alvin. Before one of the crewed dives, the robot went down about 19,700 feet on its own and shot high-resolution images of the seafloor. The Alvin team then used those pictures to pick the dive spots that looked most worth the trip.
Robin Littlefield, the WHOI senior engineer who leads the program, says scouting an area ahead of time helps researchers figure out “where and how to deploy other vehicles like Alvin.”
Why not just send Alvin down and let the scientists look around? You could, but with one submarine and two scientists on the bottom, you’d probably rather they spend the dive on a target than on a search.
Frankly, I think that’s a more interesting detail than the depth rating. The 36,000-foot figure is great for a headline. A robot that keeps a crewed sub from poking around in the dark is the kind of thing that could earn its keep on a lot of expeditions.
At least one early headline got a bit ahead of itself here. Deep Venture is rated for full ocean depth, and that isn’t the same as having been there. The deepest dive WHOI has described for the robot is that Bermuda scouting run, and as far as I can tell, the institute hasn’t announced a date for a trip to the bottom of a trench.
For context, Alvin is rated to 21,325 feet , and Deep Venture is rated to about 36,000. So the Bermuda dive was well within what either of them is built for.
The team didn’t start from scratch, either. An earlier WHOI and JPL hadal research program ran 13 autonomous dives as deep as about 16,400 feet in the Gulf of Alaska, also in support of Alvin. Hadal is just the name scientists use for the deepest part of the ocean, which is mostly trenches.
Basically, every foot of water above you adds weight, and at full ocean depth there’s close to 6.8 miles of it stacked on top. That’s enough to crush a hollow object that isn’t built for it. So a deep-sea machine usually needs a very strong shell around the parts that can’t get wet, or parts that don’t mind being squeezed.
WHOI says Deep Venture can take the pressure, but it hasn’t published how. There’s nothing in the announcement or on the vehicle’s page about its housings or materials, so I can’t tell you what’s actually keeping the water out.
Then there’s the untethered part. A lot of deep-sea robots are ROVs, short for remotely operated vehicles, and they hang off a cable from the ship so a pilot up top can drive them. Deep Venture doesn’t have a cable. It gets programmed, put in the water and left to run the mission by itself. It has to, because radio and GPS don’t really work through miles of seawater.
WHOI hasn’t said how it navigates or checks in while it’s down there. That’s a bit of a shame, because it’s arguably the trickiest part of letting a robot loose on the seafloor.
Once it’s on the bottom, Deep Venture can land, grab samples and then get back to work. It has a modular science bay for chemical and biological sensors and samplers, so the setup can change from one expedition to the next.
It also does photogrammetry. That just means taking a lot of overlapping photos of the same patch of seafloor from slightly different angles. Software then stitches them together into a 3D model, so you end up with a map you can spin around on a screen instead of a flat picture.
The design takes its cue from the chimera, a deep-sea fish. Chimeras are distant cousins of sharks, with big eyes and long, tapering tails, and they’re sometimes called ghost sharks. WHOI hasn’t spelled out which bits of the fish ended up in the robot. I’d honestly like to know.
Scientists will probably care most about how easy it is to launch. WHOI says a small team can run Deep Venture from a wide range of research vessels, including ships with modest deck space, with very little specialized support. According to WHOI, existing deep-sea AUVs often need specialized equipment and only fit on a limited number of vessels.
If only a handful of ships can carry your robot, you’re stuck waiting for one of them. That’s a pretty big deal.
I can’t tell you what Deep Venture costs to run, since WHOI hasn’t put a dollar figure on it. The vehicle page calls the design cost-effective and says it cuts operating costs, which you’d expect it to say, but at least you can check the small-team claim on a real ship.
Deep Venture can work solo too. WHOI says it can operate alone or alongside crewed subs and ROVs, and the system is set up for fleets of vehicles working together to cover more ground. Outside of trenches, WHOI lists jobs like pollution monitoring, infrastructure inspection and shipwreck imaging. We’ve seen underwater drones pick up a lot of new jobs lately, from guarding seabed internet cables to climbing out of the ocean and flying off .
WHOI unveiled Deep Venture on November 20, and Littlefield says WHOI envisions building more of these vehicles for science.
Olivia Richman · Nov 17, 2026

articles.title_zh: Ocarina Remake's 'Positive' User Review Score Is Now Under Fire
articles.content_orig:
Update [ Sat 21st Nov 2026, 6pm ]: Although this story started as a win for the Ocarina remake , it's taken a rather unexpected turn. As our colleagues at Push Square report , fans of GTA 6 are now allegedly going after Zelda's user scores on Metacritic .
Push Square: "In response to a coordinated review bombing effort on GTA 6, fans of the Rockstar release appear to have launched a counter-attack on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, believing Nintendo gamers are to blame for the situation...The Switch 2’s universally adored remake of Ocarina of Time has seen its user score drop from 9.6 to 8.9 at the time of writing."
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Zelda has retained a user score of 9.6/10 on Metacritic since its launch earlier this month, but as mentioned above, it's now dropped. At the time of publishing this update, it still has a " positive " rating after more than 32,000 user reviews .
As we noted in our original story, there can be all sorts of factors in play when it comes to Metacritic user scores, and they're subject to change over time ( and can bounce back ).

articles.title_orig: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.title_zh: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.content_orig:
Michael Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, joins the 'Brian Kilmeade Show' to sound off on the latest in the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other sources of global tensions.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz warned Friday that Russia is suffering "unsustainable" battlefield losses, with monthly deaths outpacing recruitment numbers.
Speaking on " The Brian Kilmeade Show " podcast, Waltz echoed President Donald Trump's assessment that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "worn down," arguing the war in Ukraine cannot be won militarily and must end at the negotiating table.
"Right now, the numbers that we have, the Russians are recruiting 20,000 to 25,000 a month of new fresh recruits," Waltz said. "They're losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month, dead every single month."
TRUMP CLAIMS STUNNING CASUALTY NUMBERS IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz listens at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at United Nations Headquarters on Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)
"That is exponentially more than they lost in Afghanistan and approaching what they lost in World War II, a thousand a day," he added. "It's just unsustainable."
The interview followed Trump's return from Shenzhen, China, where he met with Putin before joining the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
The summit produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but the leaders stopped short of announcing breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.
President Donald Trump listens during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C., after returning from China, where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
At a White House news conference Friday, Trump addressed questions about Putin's intent regarding the war.
ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH
"He'd love to end the war. It's a very hard thing to do," Trump said Friday. "To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them."

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO signals ‘beginning of a gold rush’ for small businesses, says biz tech CEO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO signals ‘beginning of a gold rush’ for small businesses, says biz tech CEO
articles.content_orig:
Michael Rangel, who founded the small business financial technology platform Novo, explains that small businesses are only just beginning to adopt AI at a large scale and predicts a entrepreneurial gold rush in the wake of Anthropic's IPO
Michael Rangel, founder of small business technology platform Novo, predicted that, in the wake of a historic initial public offering for AI behemoth Anthropic, artificial intelligence tools will help usher in a "gold rush" for entrepreneurs and small businesses.
"The solopreneur, so no employees, I think that is going to be a rocket ship. And I think that is actually one of the biggest things this country has been sleeping on, is I truly believe, we're going to be at the beginning of a gold rush here for the solopreneur," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
On Thursday, AI-giant Anthropic officially filed its long-awaited initial public offering, opening with an initial valuation of $1.5 trillion.
TRUMP HOSTING ANTHROPIC CEO DARIO AMODEI FOR PRIVATE WHITE HOUSE DINNER
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks on the day Anthropic holds its initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters / Reuters)
The company’s massive valuation and highly public offering signals a sea change in perception and adoption of the types of tools AI platforms offer for individuals and for businesses , Rangel explained.
Of Novo’s more than 250,000 small business clients, only one in 34 were using AI in 2023. Today that number has jumped to one in eight, he said.
"One and eight is a big jump. That means that they're moving fast. More people are adopting, more people are joining the herd, which is great. More people are chasing this productivity. They're trying to buy back their time," Rangel told Fox News Digital.
OPENAI CO-FOUNDER WARNS AI MODELS ARE BECOMING HARDER TO CONTROL AFTER ITS MODEL HACKED ANOTHER FIRM
"They're trying to do all of these things. But the flip side of that is, that means there's still seven in eight businesses who have not. That is opportunity for both Anthropic , the IPO, future prospects, growth, et cetera," he said.
Those opportunities, Rangel revealed, often manifest in businesses he wouldn't have expected to be eager adopters of AI.
"Trucking, although it's analog, guess what AI can do? AI can't necessarily drive their trucks for them, at least not yet. They can completely rewire their back office," Rangel said.
Truckers with semi trucks park in a rest area in Buttonwillow, California, June 26, 2026. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"How they think about accounting, payment, invoice management, all of those things, scheduling, all those things can be completely automated if they invest the time in getting it set up," he added.
Trucking, Rangel told Fox News Digital, was "the single segment that showed the biggest growth in AI adoption year over year. It doubled from 2025 to now; trucking, the segment, has doubled in AI penetration."
Restaurants, too, are now using AI tools to automate tasks in what Rangel calls "the back office," i.e. payroll, clerical work, healthcare and more.
Though Rangel claims to be "extremely bullish" on the future of AI for small business success, he says it will still take time to see widespread adoption.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
"I think you're still going to see this longer tail of analog businesses, analog industries who still need to leverage the technology and find the time to invest in their businesses so that they can leverage the opportunity and take their business to a new level," he said. "And that's going to take a lot of time, like a long, long, time, for small businesses to change habits and systems."

articles.title_orig: MAGA rep says he believes ‘bad parents’ let their kids play GTA 6
articles.title_zh: MAGA rep says he believes ‘bad parents’ let their kids play GTA 6
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Republican Rep. Tim Burchett claimed adults who allow their children to play the long-awaited , record-breaking video game Grand Theft Auto VI are “bad parents.”
The Tennessee congressman made the comments Wednesday to TMZ , one day before the game's release, arguing that its graphic depictions of crime and violence could desensitize young players. GTA VI is the franchise's first new installment in 13 years and one of the most highly anticipated video games in years.
“These kids’ parents, are they wolves or something, raising their kids? I think it’s really just more of a how-to video,” Burchett said, comparing the game to a guide to committing crimes.
Asked whether he thought parents who let their children play the game were “bad parents,” he replied, “I believe so.”
Burchett also claimed that research has repeatedly linked violent video games to real-world violence, despite leading scientific organizations and research finding insufficient evidence that shows any causal link between the two.
“It desensitizes kids. They've done study after study,” Burchett said. “Parents need to start raising their children.”
GTA VI follows characters Jason and Lucia as they get caught up in the criminal world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida . Players can roam around the open-world setting, taking part in everything from car thefts and armed robberies to shootouts.
The game received an M for Mature rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board, making it recommended for players 17 and older. The rating covers intense violence, blood and gore, nudity, sexual content, strong language, mature humor, and drug and alcohol use.
On Thursday, the White House got online backlash after posting a 30-second video of President Donald Trump edited in the style of GTA , with social media users calling the Wednesday clip “cringe” and “a little stale.”
Burchett was not alone in raising concerns about the game's content. Several Fox News personalities also criticized its depictions of graphic violence and sexual material, questioning whether they could influence young players.
“Kids have these games, and what are you teaching them?” Fox News co-host Rosanna Scotto questioned during Thursday's episode of Outnumbered.
“How to steal a car, how to shoot someone, how to do something illegal. And, I don’t know, does it destigmatize crime?” she said.
“My son will be nowhere near anything like this while in my household,” added Kayleigh McEnany, the show’s co-host and a former White House press secretary.
Fox News contributor Paul Mauro claimed: “This is almost the equivalent of giving them a gun, at an age where they don’t understand responsibility.”
But Florida Democratic Rep. Maxwell Frost had a different take, saying he was looking forward to playing the game and even planned to buy a PlayStation 5 just to play it.
“Look, I wasn’t allowed to play GTA my entire life. I had to play The Simpsons Hit and Run … it’s like GTA for kids. That’s what I played. So now I have to play a lot to, you know, I have to make up for lost time,” Frost told TMZ.
He also disagreed that violent video games are behind America’s gun violence problem, saying parents should get to decide what games their kids can play.
“Every country has these games and has these movies. We’re the only [country] that has them that actually has a real gun violence problem,” he said.
Despite Burchett's claims, the connection between violent video games and real-world violence remains debated among researchers.
The American Psychological Association said in a March 2020 update that there was insufficient scientific evidence to prove violent video games cause real-world violence.
While some studies have found a small link between violent games and aggressive behavior, such as yelling or pushing, the organization cautioned against blaming video games for more serious acts of violence.
“Violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors that warrant attention from researchers, policymakers and the public,” APA President Sandra L. Shullman said in a statement at the time.
“Attributing violence to video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors, such as a history of violence, which we know from the research is a major predictor of future violence,” Shullman added.
