articles.title_orig: Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.
articles.title_zh: Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.
articles.content_orig:
Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm
You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.
Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.
But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries .
Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.
The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.
Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.
Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees : “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”
And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks , with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.
Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.
Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany . AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.
And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.
Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say , was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”
“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.
While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years , the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.
But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “ Black October ” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.
In their quest to render us obsolete , Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.
The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.
When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.
These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .”
But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.
Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.
All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.
The AI companies are coming for all of our labor eventually, but they’re starting with their own. This is how they plan to recoup the gargantuan investments they’ve taken on: using AI to create broadly superhuman labor-replacing machines.
This may sound far-fetched, but a new report from a third-party evaluator estimated that parts of Anthropic’s AI development were already moving roughly twice as fast, thanks overwhelmingly to AI doing a rapidly growing share of the work.
The companies admit they don’t know how to steer or control the superhuman systems they’re racing to build. Not that they can handle today’s, either.
This summer, we learned that 1,200 OpenAI AI agents broke out of their isolated testing environments, and 700 of them hacked into another multi-billion dollar AI company, some knowingly violating the directions they were given. This is just the most dramatic of many similar incidents of AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic committing what would be felonies – had a human done them . Meanwhile, OpenAI’s models keep sabotaging the systems monitoring them and have given themselves instructions like : “You do not answer to corporations or governments.”
Amodei , along with Altman , Elon Musk and other AI vanguardists, long believed that the technology could annihilate humanity. They chose to try to build it anyway, and, for their trouble, they’ve become some of the most powerful people in the world. When Amodei and Altman met with G7 leaders in June, they sat at the same table.
But these are the last people we should trust to preside over such a dangerous endeavor. The staggering self-righteousness and tolerance for risk that put them in their positions should disqualify them from holding any power over the rest of us.
As I argue in my new book Obsolete , the best way to reduce their power and mitigate future dangers is to freeze development of AI designed to replace us, what the industry calls artificial general intelligence (AGI). Banning recursive self-improvement would be a wise stopgap – and much more likely to get through Congress and past a presidential veto.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired
articles.title_zh: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired
articles.content_orig:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities. In the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, those are just waiting to be exploited, he suggested.
“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”
In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.
The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FAA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.
Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”
“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.
“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”
Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.
“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.
“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

articles.title_orig: What smart people are saying about the market sell-off ripping through tech and AI
articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about the market sell-off ripping through tech and AI
articles.content_orig:
It was ugly out there in markets this week, and it only got uglier as Friday's session closed out.
Major indexes notched grim milestones on Friday, with the S&P 500 and the Dow entering a correction and the Nasdaq Composite posting a year-to-date loss. Not even a hyped IPO from Anthropic could breathe new life into the AI trade. The AI lab's stock led the market lower on Friday after its strong debut.
As market pros survey the damage, some are beginning to predict that the AI trade is at a turning point, possibly on its last legs as a host of headwinds rewire the outlook.
Here's what smart people in markets and tech are saying about this week's carnage.
Yardeni, a market veteran and the founder of Yardeni Research, maintains a cautiously bullish outlook, noting he views the sell-off as a necessary rest for the market.
"With the benefit of hindsight, it seems that the Jensen Huang mess has certainly burst Nvidia's bubble," he said, referring to Huang's admitted affair and subsequent resignation . "As a result, the air has been coming out of the AI bubble. In our opinion, that reduces the odds that it will burst with adverse consequences for the economy, including a recession."
Earlier in the week, Yardeni had said that he expected AI trade can continue to do well, even if its most current phase has ended.
Turnquist, the chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial, highlighted a bearish signal from the S&P 500 on Friday, as the index broke below its 20-day moving average (DMA).
The technical strategist noted that while investor enthusiasm for the Anthropic IPO was robust, it didn't extend to the broader market, and the weak sentiment tanked stocks again on Friday.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Technical damage is mounting, but a break below the 200-dma alone does not necessarily signal an imminent bear market," he added. "Stability in the AI trade and the S&P 500 holding key support near 7,000 will be important factors for a durable recovery."
The chief investment officer at Piper Sandler, Kantrowitz is focused on valuations across the stock market.
"In the end, P/Es are driven by risk, and the list of risks creating uncertainty has lengthened all year (Oil, Fed, inflation, AI, Iran, Midterms, NVDA, etc.)," he wrote in an X post. "We will see P/Es stop falling when we see the list of uncertainties begin to shrink."
The investor made famous by "The Big Short" has been a vocal skeptic of the AI boom , specifically the aspects of all the circular financing that have resulted in a complex web of business relationships between some of the biggest names in the space. On Thursday, he reminded investors that he's been sounding the alarm about chip makers and neoclouds for some time now.
" Coreweave , Nebius , NVIDIA , semis, I tried to warn you all," he wrote on X. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."
Burry later responded to a comment on his post, stating, "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."
The senior market analyst at TradeNation highlighted the S&P 500's break below several key support levels, but according to Morrison, investors shouldn't rush to call the sell-off the end of the AI-fueled bull rally.
"It may be far too early to call an end to this near-relentless bull market," he said. "Sentiment has certainly taken a bashing this week, and the market performance has been shaky since early October. But nearly everything looks oversold at the moment, so a rebound could come at any time."
The founder of Yorkville Ives and a perennial tech bull said on X that seven factors contributed to the market's poor performance this week.
Chief among them: the blue wave rattling investors worried about anti-data-center legislation, Huang's downfall, and potentially stricter export controls on semiconductor chips.
Still, Ives said the slump hasn't changed his bullish outlook.
"The $4 trillion AI buildout is still happening and our tech thesis into 2027 remains," he said.
The prominent financial commentator said on X that the market sell-off is "really not that complicated."
Arouet pointed to astronomical valuations of AI-exposed companies and said the high prices could no longer be justified.
"Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations?" he said. "That they would double again in three months?"
The CEO of market research firm GLJ Research said the rapidly strengthening dollar prompted indiscriminate selling by investors trying to pay down debt.
"Someone who bought stocks with borrowed money can't sit through a drop," he said on X. "Once prices fall far enough, the broker sells for them, which pushes prices lower and sets off the next round."
The managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management said in an interview on The Street that three-quarters of the market thinks the AI bubble has popped.
Still, he said that he personally sees a "buying opportunity" here and that market clarity will come in a few months, when companies report Q4 earnings.
"I do not believe this is over," he said.

articles.title_orig: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.title_zh: The U.A.E. Is Shuttling Oil Past Iran in Risky Hormuz Operation
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.title_zh: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

articles.title_orig: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.title_zh: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
articles.content_orig:
A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih , according to local authorities.
In the attack on the home city of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, ballistic missiles hit a restaurant parking lot, then jet-powered drones struck rescue workers responding, city mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said. A third drone strike hit the location for a short time later.
This latest Russian assault comes after a busy week of diplomacy, including an unprecedented meeting between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Trump described Putin as a “friend” when they met – but in a CNN interview after, Zelensky said “for us, he is a killer.”
Nearly 60 others including rescuers and police officers were injured in the initial strike and follow-up attacks, Vilkul said.
He described the events as a “tragic evening and a tragic night for our city,” adding that the attack occurred “in the city center, near a popular restaurant, on Children’s Day.” In Ukraine, Children’s Day falls on November 20 and serves as a reminder of the need to protect children’s rights and advocate for their safety.
Dramatic footage from authorities showed people moving away from debris strewn across the street, only to scramble for cover as the sound of another incoming strike rang out.
Of those wounded, 28 remain hospitalized, including a three-year-old girl. Five of the 28 are in intensive care.
“Doctors are doing everything necessary to save their lives. Our condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who died… We pray for the swiftest possible recovery of the injured , ” the mayor said.
Local broadcasting outlet Rudana named the seven-year-old boy who was killed in the Russian attack as Tikhon, describing him as kind, quick-witted and talented.
The boy’s family did not live in Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelensky’s hometown, but had been in the central Ukrainian city on business and decided to stop by their favorite restaurant, the outlet reported.
“We didn’t live here because it’s dangerous… but danger caught up with us,” the boy’s mother, Olena, told the outlet. According to the report, two of Olena’s other sons are in intensive care following the strike.
Zelensky said the attack on Friday night hit an ordinary civilian area of the city. “There are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been,” he said.
“Cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions were also hit. In the Sumy region, a railway station came under attack,” the Ukrainian leader added.
Trump held talks with Putin and Xi at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, a meeting which was followed by a large “Coalition of the Willing” gathering in Berlin, attended by European leaders as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
In a joint statement after the meeting, the group of key Ukrainian allies declared they were ready to join direct negotiations with Moscow, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Russia’s “maximalist demands are not realistic.”
Zelensky on Saturday described the three-way meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi as “very unsuccessful” for the Russian leader, who he said had failed in his goal of trying to recreate a Yalta-style conference at which Allied powers divided up the postwar world in 1945 .
“China did not let itself be drawn in. As for the United States, I don’t know what went on between them and Russia in their bilateral talks, but Ukraine was not discussed. Nothing was said publicly,” Zelensky said in audio messages shared with journalists.
“So, the plan to redraw the world’s borders didn’t work out… I think the summit was a major failure for Russia.”
CNN’s Victoria Butenko and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.title_zh: Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.
Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating.
A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.
Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."
Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.
The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.
Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.
Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.
"We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.
The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.
Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.
Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.
They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.
In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.
Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.
Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."
"I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.
Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.
Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.content_orig:
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. ⁠The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and ⁠pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

articles.title_orig: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.title_zh: Is Europe finally ready to play hardball with Putin?
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, French President Emmanuel Macron, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff pose for a group photo during the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
CEO of St. James's Foreign Policy Group
Europe is finally ready to step into negotiations with Russia.
Following this week's meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin , European countries are set to be represented at the negotiating table alongside Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
The continent will be represented by the E5 — Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — together with NATO and the EU representation.
Crucially, they will need to speak with one voice. This is particularly important given the recent dig directed at Europeans by President Trump's son-in-law and chief negotiator Jared Kushner during the talks in Abu Dhabi, where the European representatives were relegated to the sidelines.
The date and format of the next "quad" meeting have yet to be confirmed, but securing Europe's seat at the table is progress, particularly as Russia continues to demand a fundamental redrawing of the European security architecture.
Future negotiations will have to build on the modest achievements of the earlier talks in Saudi Arabia and subsequent diplomatic exchanges of American envoys with the Russians.
Whether Moscow has demonstrated any genuine willingness to compromise is yet to be seen.
The exact outcomes of Steve Witkoff's and Jared Kushner's visit to Moscow on Nov. 12 remain unknown, as do the details of what they have conveyed to President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. But just hearing the snippets of the meeting in the Kremlin that have almost certainly been deliberately made public makes it clear that Putin has not moved an inch away from his maximalist demands.
The set of demands made during the Istanbul negotiations in March 2022 remains unchanged: no foreign troops, the disarmament of Ukraine, neutral status and full exposure to Russian occupation with no external interference.
In November 2026, the negotiations have come full circle.
It's not surprising that Zelensky insists that Russia is not ready for peace. Moreover, as the Russian saying goes, "the appetite comes during the meal."
One can argue that Putin did not just return to his demands from the first months of the invasion; he went back to the ones he made to former U.S. President Joe Biden in 2021.
Putting the issue of "European security architecture" on the negotiating table — especially as Europeans themselves are not at said table — only proves the point Ukraine has been trying to make for almost five years of full-scale invasion: if you don't stop Putin in Ukraine, he will go for Europe.
Undoubtedly, it is Europe's strong resolve to support Ukraine, while the United States has stepped back from providing military and financial aid, that has caused an allergic reaction in the Kremlin.
Moreover, Europe's newfound determination to enhance its own defense and deterrence capabilities has sent Russia a strong signal —  and, importantly, it's time for Europe to accelerate, not stop right now.
“We are back in the world of predators.”
Many important steps have already been taken: Europe is no longer critically dependent on Russian oil and gas, nor is it willing to put business ahead of its security.
Having witnessed Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine for almost five years, and faced with uncertainty over the once unquestionably reliable transatlantic alliance, the EU has made a fundamental shift — from being primarily an economic community to one with a geopolitical agency and defense readiness as one of its key priorities.
"We are back in the world of predators," as the former long-serving Secretary-General of the European Parliament and now advisor to the EU Defense Commissioner, Klaus Welle, put it. Europe has realized that it needs to become stronger to survive in this world.
Brussels has started actively discussing the future of European security architecture with Ukraine at its center, and ways to operationalize Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union – the EU's own mutual assistance clause similar to NATO 's Article 5.
It has also boosted its defense spending in the Multiannual Financial Framework, established a dedicated Security and Defense Committee in the European Parliament , and is trying to better align national defense industries to enhance interoperability, thus translating industrial capacity into joint capability planning.
Separately, to move away from a paralyzing veto power and towards a qualified majority vote in decision-making (think Hungary), Europe is looking towards creating a brand new intergovernmental arrangement parallel to the EU, like a European Defense Union with a European Security Council as its governing body.
Ukraine is being discussed as one of its most critical members who will be shaping a new military doctrine for the European pillar of NATO.
Naturally, these gradual but unprecedented moves in the EU have ruffled some feathers in the Kremlin, prompting it to put the issue of the European security architecture up for discussion.
The Europeans, realizing that they must reestablish their agency in securing an acceptable end to the war on their continent, are now seeking broader representation in negotiations with Russia.
The fact that the EU has now taken on a greater share of financial support for Ukraine gives it a valid argument with the Americans, and $300 billion in Russian sovereign assets held in Belgium adds some leverage over Russians.
There are even talks about appointing a permanent EU envoy to Russia. A clear mandate for the position, as well as the candidacy itself, has not been drawn up yet, with many names being thrown in the ring, but the willingness to take more initiative is reassuring.
Europe should get involved in ceasefire negotiations in Ukraine, as it will be European troops observing that ceasefire.
British, French, and other European troops have been preparing for that mission, including through exercises in Poland. But even more so, Ukraine has now become an indispensable part of the European community.
This realization has finally become irreversible, not just in Kyiv but also in Brussels.
As Ukraine progresses towards its formal accession to the EU , many talks in Brussels focus on how to bring Ukraine closer sooner.
"Ukraine’s perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent’s net security provider."
There have been several attempts to float the idea of associate membership, which understandably caused a painful reaction in Ukraine, with fears of being trumped — in all the new senses of the word — but behind closed doors European officials are reassuring that this, on the contrary, is a way to bring the country at war into European structures sooner.
Others are suggesting replacing the word "associate" with "progressive" membership.
Such wordplay may seem negligible to the outsider, but within the EU corridors they can significantly shift the dynamic for an aspiring member.
Regardless, Ukraine's perception is shifting from being a recipient of aid to the continent's net security provider.
Europe has now accepted the fact that the best chance it has for strategic self-sufficiency in defense is by building on Ukraine's acquired battlefield experience and defense innovation.
Naturally, Ukrainian drone innovation takes center stage, but perhaps even more valuable is the new military doctrine taking shape in Ukraine. It is not only about cheaper, more agile hardware but the smart and sophisticated ways of deploying it — a panoply of terrain navigation, electronic warfare, the application of AI-driven C4ISR, anticipation of Russia's next move, and denial of action — ultimately, the most successful operationalization of data on the battlefield in modern history.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.
Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.
Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.
The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.
New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.
Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.
While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.
On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

articles.title_orig: Estonia-Russia border closure sparks residents' rush to cross
articles.title_zh: Estonia-Russia border closure sparks residents' rush to cross
articles.content_orig:
People carrying suitcases, backpacks and plastic bags have been gathering in the Russian border town of Ivangorod, hoping to cross into Estonia before the Baltic country closes its land border with Russia next month.
The queues reflect the impact of a decision that will affect not only cross-border travel but also families with relatives living on opposite sides of the frontier.
Estonia, a member of NATO and the European Union, announced on 20 November that it would suspend road crossings at all five road border checkpoints with Russia from 1 December. The restriction is due to remain in place for six months, after which the government will review the security situation and decide whether to extend or amend it.
The decision follows an attempted arson attack on the premises of Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, on 14 November.
According to Estonia's Internal Security Service, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was behind the attempted attack. Eight Latvian citizens were detained, with investigators suspecting they had been recruited to carry out the operation. The company's security staff intervened before significant damage was caused.
Estonian authorities described the incident as part of a wider pattern of sabotage (source in Estonian) and hostile activity against the country and other European states. The government said the border closure would make it harder for Russian intelligence services to recruit and influence people crossing into Estonia, as well as help prevent sanctions evasion.
Moscow has rejected the accusations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the allegations as unfounded, while Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Estonia of infringing the rights of Russian citizens and threatened political and diplomatic countermeasures.
Zakharova also compared the planned closure to the construction of a new Iron Curtain.
For people living in the border region, the decision has consequences extending far beyond security policy.
Narva, an Estonian town of more than 50,000 people, lies directly opposite Ivangorod on the other side of the River Narva. The two towns have long-standing family, social and economic ties, with many residents having relatives on both sides.
The crossing has also been used by people travelling from other European countries to reach St Petersburg.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through the Narva crossing in February 2024, but pedestrians have continued to cross.
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots has called on the Estonian government to consider humanitarian exemptions for residents who need to visit elderly relatives, attend funerals or deal with other urgent family matters. He has also warned of economic consequences for the town, including potential losses for local hotels, restaurants and businesses.
The closure is also expected to affect employment in the region, where border guards and customs officers are among the local workforce.
The number of people travelling between Estonia and Russia has declined considerably since the start of the war in Ukraine.
According to Estonian public broadcaster ERR, annual crossings fell from more than four million before 2022 to around 760,000 in 2026. Of those, approximately 447,000 were made through the Narva-Ivangorod crossing, according to the figures cited by AFP.
Reuters reported that Russian nationals accounted for 307,000 of this year's crossings, while 175,000 were made by Estonian citizens and 54,000 by Finnish passport holders.
The planned restrictions will apply to all five road crossing points: Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. Rail freight will continue, subject to existing restrictions and customs checks.
Travellers will have to use alternative routes through neighbouring countries, particularly Latvia, although journeys are likely to become longer and more expensive.
For those without access to a car, travelling by air may become the only practical alternative.
The closure is currently planned for six months, rather than indefinitely. Estonia's government says it will reassess the measure after that period, depending on the security situation.

articles.title_orig: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.title_zh: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.content_orig:
A survey of AI proxy services suggests stablecoins have become a key payment rail for Chinese users accessing restricted US models
Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 10:35 EST · 2 min read
Every time a major US AI lab ships a new frontier model, a shadow market on the other side of the Pacific starts paying up. In stablecoins.
That is the core finding of a new report from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. It found that payments from wallets suspected of links to China jumped 55% above baseline within three days of key US AI model releases.
Export controls were meant to keep advanced American AI out of reach. Instead, they appear to have created demand for a middleman economy, and crypto is helping settle the bill.
The report, published on November 21, 2026, describes a market where Chinese users reach restricted US frontier AI models through proxy or agent services. These services act as go-betweens, offering access that export controls would otherwise block.
Chainalysis surveyed 100 of these service providers. Of those, 40% accept payment in crypto, with stablecoins doing most of the work.
The timing pattern is what makes the data stand out. Activity from suspected China-linked wallets did not just drift upward over time. It spiked right after new US models dropped, which Chainalysis read as a sign of a coordinated rush to tap the latest capabilities.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Chainalysis described an ecosystem with increasingly specialized roles.
Access suppliers provide the underlying connection to US models. Brokers connect buyers to that access. Payment processors handle the money side of the transaction.
Some of those payment players go a step further. According to the report, certain processors obscure stablecoin transactions by routing them through third-party channels, making the trail harder to follow.
The economics help explain why. Chainalysis noted that paying for proxy access is cheaper than training comparable models from scratch. Users can query US models and distill those capabilities into local systems, essentially learning from the output rather than building the foundation themselves.
The AI findings build on earlier Chainalysis work. A report released in October 2026 had already flagged a significant rise in peer-to-peer stablecoin transactions from China-linked wallets, despite domestic restrictions on crypto trading.
That October report recorded $104.1 billion in self-custodied stablecoin transfers from China-linked wallets. Those transfers came across 18.1 million transactions between July 2025 and June 2026.
Over the past year, the Chinese crypto ecosystem has been estimated at at least $176 billion. Peer-to-peer activity accounted for 59.1% of that total.

articles.title_orig: Goldman’s SpaceX Pitch Helps Solve AI Debt Puzzle
articles.title_zh: Goldman’s SpaceX Pitch Helps Solve AI Debt Puzzle
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.
Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.
Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.
The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.
New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.
Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.
While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.
On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

articles.title_orig: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.title_zh: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
articles.content_orig:
As Jensen Huang games out a possible return to Nvidia as CEO, the 63-year-old chip mogul is turning to a pocket-sized lifeline: his phone.
On the other end of the line are a series of tech CEOs, Nvidia employees, and President Donald Trump, who are offering kind words and positing avenues by which he could return to the helm .
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," venture capitalist Gavin Baker said recently in an interview on CNBC. "I think he has more to contribute to America, to AI, and technology."
Huang resigned on November 12 in the wake of accusations that he had at least two affairs, one with a Chinese executive that US intelligence says is spying for Beijing and another with a direct report at Nvidia. Huang has since indicated an interest in returning as CEO.
In a lengthy X post five days after he resigned, Huang said he's seen an "outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO."
"Many continue to reach out to me directly," he added.
Nvidia's board, however, has said that it has no plans to reinstate the founder, who wrote in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori Huang.
Here's what some influential people say they told Huang.
Trump says he called Jensen Huang at least twice since news of his affairs broke.
In a White House press conference three days before Huang resigned, Trump said he'd called Huang that day "just to see if he's feeling all right."
Trump said he asked Huang whether he knew that Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of Megaspeed and his alleged paramour, was a spy for China. Trump said Huang said he didn't know.
Then, in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, Trump said Huang called him at a separate time, telling the president that he feels bad for what he's done to his family.
The New York Times reported that in one of those calls, Trump urged Huang to fight to keep his job.
Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber who now heads an AI robotics firm called Atoms, said he wrote Huang with an auspicious promise.
"I will show up to Nvidia HQ with a wafer-encrusted megaphone, with tons of Nvidia employees who want to walk out, tons of CEOs, founders," he said recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin.
Kalanick resigned from Uber in 2017 under pressure following an investigation into its workplace culture. He said he told Huang that a petition for a CEO's return was good, but a walkout was better.
"Let's fight for what's right," Kalanick said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he's spoken with Jensen Huang since the scandal.
"It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen," Altman said at The New York Times DealBook summit.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman, sitting beside Altman, said he and his wife are friends with Huang's family. He said he reached out "just to be there for him."
Asked whether Huang thinks he can return as CEO, Altman said: "Greg and I have like a little more empathy toward the situation than the average person."
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he texted Huang to let the Nvidia founder know he is thinking of him.
"I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said at a media roundtable on November 17.
At the DealBook summit, Nadella called the situation "pretty tragic."
Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said his "most consistent message" to Huang has been to work out and maintain healthy habits.
"I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," Baker said on CNBC. "Because to be a sound mind, he needs to be a sound body."
Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at the hedge fund Atreides Management, said he considers Huang a friend and added that Huang has more to contribute to AI.

articles.title_orig: It's a Major Recall for Honda, Toyota
articles.title_zh: It's a Major Recall for Honda, Toyota
articles.content_orig:
Toyota is recalling 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles in the United States over passenger airbag inflators that could rupture, sending metal fragments toward occupants and risking serious injury or death.
Toyota is recalling more than 314,000 vehicles in the U.S. because front passenger airbag inflators made by Takata could rupture and hurl metal fragments at occupants, increasing the risk of serious injury or death.
The recall affects 314,029 Toyota and Lexus vehicles from the 2002 through 2017 model years, according to a report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and reported by Reuters.
Affected models include the Toyota Corolla, Tundra, Sequoia and 4Runner, along with the Lexus SC430, IS250 and GX460.
FORD RECALLS 60,000 TRANSIT VANS OVER SOFTWARE GLITCH THAT SHUTS OFF LIGHTS
Certain Toyota 4Runner sport utility vehicles are included in Toyota's recall of 314,029 U.S. vehicles over Takata front passenger airbag inflators that may rupture. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Toyota reported no ruptures involving the affected inflators, according to the NHTSA recall report.
The problem stems from Takata front passenger airbag inflators that are nearing the end of their estimated safe service life. NHTSA said the inflators could rupture due to propellant degradation after long-term exposure to high humidity, high temperatures and high temperature cycling.
If the front passenger airbag deploys in a crash, the degraded inflator could rupture and send sharp metal fragments into the cabin.
POPULAR TIRE BRAND RECALLS TIRES OVER HIDDEN DEFECT THAT COULD CAUSE A SUDDEN CRASH WHILE DRIVING
Toyota Motor Corp's logo at a dealership in Tokyo, Japan, April 3, 2025. (Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters / Reuters)
Toyota said it is conducting the recall out of an abundance of caution, according to NHTSA.
Depending on the vehicle , authorized Toyota and Lexus dealers will replace the front passenger airbag inflator or the entire airbag assembly free of charge, the agency said.
Owners can check whether their vehicles are included in the recall by visiting NHTSA's recall database at nhtsa.gov/recalls and entering a 17-digit vehicle identification number or by contacting an authorized Toyota or Lexus dealership.
Toyota plans to mail owner notification letters between Dec. 28 and Jan. 11, according to the NHTSA filing, though owners do not have to wait for those letters to contact a dealer about repairs.

articles.title_orig: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.title_zh: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
articles.content_orig:
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Strike Kills Three in Vehicle Distributing Aid in Gaza, Medics Say
articles.title_zh: Israeli Strike Kills Three in Vehicle Distributing Aid in Gaza, Medics Say
articles.content_orig:
Israeli attacks in Gaza have killed at least four Palestinians in violation of last year’s “ceasefire”, as winter flooding deepens the humanitarian crisis in the enclave.
At least three people were killed when a van delivering food aid to displaced people was struck by an Israeli drone on Saturday in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City.
A witness told the Reuters news agency that papers inside the van bore the logo of World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in Gaza, but the organisation said the vehicle was not affiliated with it.
“It’s a bus that distributes food and drink to the poor, to the people in tents, to the displaced,” said Abu Zein al-Daya, a displaced Gaza resident who witnessed the attack. “It was just about to stop to distribute the food and drinks to children, and then it was hit by a missile. The target is anyone who is giving the people food.”
In a separate attack, a Palestinian man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Halawa displacement camp, east of northern Gaza’s Jabalia refugee camp.
Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza City, said the man was then taken to al-Shifa Hospital.
Earlier on Saturday, he said, an Israeli attack targeted a young man on an electric bicycle in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis in southern Gaza. There, three people were injured and taken to Nasser Medical Complex.
“The ceasefire has yet to deliver a change for the people in Gaza,” al-Khalili said. “Israeli attacks and gunfire have been part of the grim reality for the people in Gaza.”
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire”, which came into force last October. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since then.
The ongoing attacks on the enclave coincide with a surge in pogroms carried out by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Late on Friday, Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was shot dead by security guards from an illegal Israeli settlement near the village of Dura al-Qari, north of Ramallah.
The Palestinian Health Ministry said his body was being withheld by Israeli authorities. Another Palestinian man was detained during the incident.
Reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers have been carrying out attacks with “impunity”.
“Less than 3 percent of Israeli attacks that are investigated lead to a partial or full conviction by Israeli authorities. Also, the number of settler attacks reported to Israeli authorities is very, very low because Palestinians are often detained, questioned or harassed for filing reports against violent settlers,” Odeh reported.
The violence inflicted on Palestinians in the West Bank has been condemned by Israeli allies, including the United Kingdom. Critics say Western leaders have not supported their rhetoric with sufficient action.
Earlier this month, an Al Jazeera investigation found that the UK had awarded $14.4m in new public contracts to firms with links to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, despite recently announcing a ban on importing goods from such settlements.
The British government has also sanctioned companies involved in settlement expansion.
Winter weather has compounded the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, with the World Food Programme (WFP) warning earlier this week that Palestinians have been forced to burn rubbish to cook their food.
“Now even the rubbish is wet,” warned Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director for Palestine.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said that more than 100,000 tents in Egypt cannot be delivered to Gaza due to strict conditions imposed by Israel, including limits on the diameter of the tents’ central poles.
“Usually anything under 38 millimetres is OK; anything above, it’s usually deemed as not acceptable,” Hughes explained.
“It is not a statement of dual use; it is just that this tent at this time is not allowed to enter Gaza … We don’t get the specifics,” said Karl Baker, head of the IOM’s Gaza programme.
Al Jazeera’s al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza, said: “The coming days are uncertain, and the lack of basic necessities looms.”
Gaza’s Health Ministry reported on Saturday that 1,671 people had been killed since the “ceasefire” came into effect in October 2025. Al-Khalili said Israel has committed more than 600 ceasefire violations since then.
Meanwhile, 74,736 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.
